title: Rochdale veterans' group drove to Bournemouth and housed veteran who had lived in a tent for 14 months
excerpt: Get Together After Serving found a veteran a hotel room within 20 minutes and a home the next day, paid for by the Denehurst Café welfare fund.
body:
A Rochdale veterans' group used its Denehurst Café welfare fund to reach a veteran in crisis in Bournemouth, finding him a home within 24 hours.

Get Together After Serving (GTAS), which runs the café in Denehurst Park, said the veteran, Matt, had called and told them he was going to end his life. He had spent 14 months living in a tent.

Matt served for 10 years in the Armed Forces, including tours of Afghanistan, Iraq, Bosnia, Canada and Germany, according to GTAS.

GTAS said that within 20 minutes of setting off from Rochdale, the team had booked him emergency hotel accommodation so he would be safe that night.

When they arrived, they met him face to face. The next day, he was given the keys to a property owned by a veteran landlord.

The hotel and the fuel for the journey were paid for from the welfare fund at Denehurst Café, which is topped up by café sales and donations from customers.

In a statement, GTAS said: "We didn't have to delay, complete applications or wait for someone else to step in. We were able to act immediately."

Speaking to Rochdale Daily, Matt said he had been homeless for seven years on paper, and had spent the last 14 months in a tent in the Salisbury area.

He said he had been evicted under a no-fault notice from a veterans' centre. When he approached the council, he said he was told he was not a priority and was placed in shared accommodation.

He said conditions there were filthy and the atmosphere felt unsafe. It took three complaints before anything was done, he said, and nobody told him to register for Universal Credit, leaving him with £1,200 of rent arrears.

He said he went back to the tent, and that his complaint about the arrears could take up to eight months to reach a decision through the ombudsman.

Matt said a call to a veterans' mental health charity ended with his case being closed after he did not reply to a question for seven minutes.

He said his mental health worker was "fantastic" and argued from February that he should be treated as a priority for housing, but that by August he still had not been given priority.

He said that when he was admitted to hospital for his mental health, he was left in a corridor for 13 hours. He was also told that therapy could not start until he had a home.

Matt said he had contacted his local MP for eight months without result, and had pulled out his own teeth while living in the tent. He now needs 12 teeth removed.

After he posted TikTok videos about the treatment of veterans, he said a veterans' charity offered to clear his arrears, but he was told he could then face a wait of up to seven years for housing.

GTAS saw his comments online and Adam, from the group, got in touch within a week.

Matt said that on the day GTAS set off, a Salisbury reporter had called an ambulance and three paramedics came to his tent. He said the paramedics contacted the council twice and were told there was nothing available.

He said he felt huge relief when Adam rang to say he was on his way from Rochdale, and that Adam broke down in tears when he called back to say Matt would get his keys the next day.

The GTAS team took him to a hotel, then out for breakfast, and went to see the conditions he had been living in.

Matt, who worked in pest control and plans to set up his own business, said he was already back in the gym and felt at home for the first time in years. He said that since meeting Adam and Josh from GTAS he no longer felt alienated or forgotten.

GTAS said: "We would get back in that car tomorrow, and so would every member of the GTAS team."

The group said the case showed veterans in crisis should be able to get immediate help wherever they live, and that support should come before someone becomes homeless.

Matt is planning a sponsored walk to Rochdale to thank GTAS and raise money for its work.

GTAS has urged any veteran struggling with mental health, homelessness, isolation, addiction or money to contact the group through Denehurst Café. Anyone who is struggling can call Samaritans free, day or night, on 116 123.

Source: Matt speaking to Rochdale Daily, and a statement from Get Together After Serving. Photograph: supplied.
